Stages of development. Stages of development are discrete periods across the human lifespan characterized by distinct patterns of physical, cognitive, emotional, and social capabilities. Jean Piaget's theory of cognitive development proposed four major stages that fundamentally shaped developmental psychology and how we think about learning.

Piaget's sensorimotor stage from birth to two years emphasizes learning through physical interaction and movement. Infants gradually discover the world through their bodies. Early in this stage they lack object permanence, the understanding that things continue to exist even when out of sight. The preoperational stage from two to seven years marks the emergence of symbolic thinking and language, a major leap forward. But children in this stage remain egocentric, seeing the world primarily from their own perspective, and struggle with conservation tasks like understanding that the amount of liquid doesn't change when you pour it into a different shaped container. In the concrete operational stage from seven to eleven years, children can perform logical operations on concrete objects and understand conservation, but they struggle with abstract hypothetical reasoning. The formal operational stage at twelve years and older marks the capacity for abstract thinking, hypothesis testing, and formal logic, though not all adolescents or adults consistently use formal operations even when capable of doing so.

Erik Erikson proposed eight stages spanning the entire lifespan, not just childhood, each defined by a psychosocial crisis to be resolved. Stage-based models assume development is sequential, meaning you cannot skip stages, universal across all humans, and qualitatively distinct, with each stage involving different cognitive structures, not just more knowledge.

Subsequent research has challenged pure stage models. Development appears more continuous than stage theory suggests, and culture shapes developmental trajectories differently. Stage models can overemphasize discontinuity and overlook the gradual, context-dependent nature of development in real children. Individual variation within stages is substantial. Not all children develop at the same pace, and some demonstrate capacities from multiple stages simultaneously rather than fitting neatly into one. Cross-cultural research reveals that the age ranges Piaget identified are culturally variable, emerging at different ages depending on schooling, cultural practices, and exposure to formal logic.
